subject: sociology
title: Beliefs in Society: New Religious Movements & Globalisation
welcome_lead: Sects, cults and the global flow of faith.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology NRMs Wallis sects cults globalisation fundamentalism.
final_note: Religion globalises — and sometimes pushes back.

concepts.def: Small intense breakaway from established religion.
Loosely organised group, no clear orthodoxy.

walkthroughs.body_html: Wallis (1984) classified NRMs by relation to world. World-rejecting: Unification Church (Moonies), Hare Krishna — communal life, asceticism. World-accommodating: Pentecostalism — separates faith from work. World-affirming: Scientology, TM — promises success in current society.

Bruce: NRMs flourish where traditional religion declines. Wallis: 1960s counter-culture spawned world-rejecting NRMs. Stark & Bainbridge (1985): sects offer 'compensators' for life's deprivations. Most members drift away within years.

Giddens (1999): fundamentalism is a reactive response to globalisation's threats to tradition. Bauman: postmodern uncertainty drives some toward absolute truth. Pentecostalism is the world's fastest-growing religion (~280 million followers, ~25 million yearly converts).

options: The spread of fast-food principles (efficiency, calculability, predictability, control) across society.

mcqs.q: What are Weber's three dimensions of stratification?
options: Weber's three dimensions are upper, middle and working class.
Weber agreed with Marx that class is purely economic.
Class (economic position in markets), status (social honour/prestige), and party (organised power) — Weber argued these can vary independently, unlike Marx's economic-determinism view.
